> **TL;DR** Thinking Machines introduced Inkling 2 Mini using looped transformer layers to boost reasoning locally, Google opened the Genie 4 API for interactive world generation, and OpenAI tightened reasoning trace defenses in GPT-6.2 Astra.

## What actually moved today

The landscape of architectural primitives and developer APIs shifted with several official releases hitting repositories and documentation portals. Instead of relying purely on massive parameter scaling, recent updates focus on architectural efficiency like looped layers, interactive physics engines, and strict distillation countermeasures. Developers now have concrete new primitives to experiment with locally and via cloud APIs.

## The model watch

### Thinking Machines Inkling 2 Mini
Thinking Machines released **Inkling 2 Mini**, a looped transformer model featuring 26.4B total parameters and 3.4B active parameters. The core architectural change involves running the middle 12 layers three times per token during inference. This design choice increases reasoning depth without inflating the total parameter footprint, allowing the model to compete with larger systems while running locally on consumer hardware equipped with 32 GB of memory. Developers should re-run local evaluation suites focusing on multi-step reasoning tasks to see how iterative layer execution impacts throughput and latency compared to standard feed-forward topologies. Under the hood, the recurrent reuse of weights introduces unique memory-access patterns during generation, shifting bottlenecks from sheer parameter bandwidth to cache efficiency across the looped segments.

### Google Genie 4 API Access
Google opened **Genie 4** directly within the Gemini API and AI Studio. Priced at approximately $0.10 per second, the model constructs a 720p interactive world complete with synchronized audio from simple text or image prompts. Developers can now programmatically generate physics-based environments without managing custom simulation engines. You should test this endpoint by passing structured initial frames to evaluate how well the system maintains temporal consistency and physical constraints across extended interaction loops. The underlying mechanics handle complex environmental dynamics natively, though developers must account for API latency when building real-time interactive loops.

### OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra Defenses
OpenAI updated internal security controls for **GPT-6.2 Astra**, successfully reducing successful extractions of hidden reasoning traces down to 0.2% from 54% in the earlier **GPT-6 Astra**. Reasoning traces are now cryptographically and logically bound directly to the active dialogue history, preventing unauthorized side-channel extraction. This mitigation substantially thwarts adversarial distillation attempts targeting frontier reasoning capabilities. Security engineers should audit their red-teaming pipelines against these updated endpoints to verify that prompt-injection vectors can no longer bypass the tightened trace boundaries.

### MiniMind PyTorch Tutorial
An educational implementation appeared on GitHub via the **MiniMind** repository, detailing how to train a small language model completely from scratch using pure PyTorch. The guide walks through custom JSONL corpora ingestion, token masking strategies, and local deployment pipelines. It provides an accessible sandbox for developers seeking to inspect the fundamental mechanics of transformer training without abstract framework overhead. You can modify the attention heads and context windows in the repository to observe how hyperparameters directly affect convergence rates during initial pre-training stages.

### Hallmark AI Design Skill
**Hallmark** launched as an open-source design skill targeting coding agents like **Claude Code**, **Cursor**, **Codex**, and OpenCode. Utilizing a curated set of 50 design themes, the skill guides AI agents to construct distinctive, non-generic web layouts and automatically audits codebases for repetitive aesthetic clichés. Developers integrating autonomous coding agents into frontend workflows can plug this skill in to enforce varied UI patterns and avoid cookie-cutter outputs. The system inspects DOM structures and CSS properties iteratively during generation to correct stylistic drift before final rendering.

### Cairn State-Space Search
**Cairn** debuted as a general-purpose AI state-space search system, initially demonstrated within automated penetration testing frameworks. It provides structured graph exploration capabilities designed for complex, branching decision tasks where traditional heuristic search falls short. Engineers working on automated agent loops can evaluate **Cairn** to manage complex exploration spaces, replacing ad-hoc search scripts with a dedicated state-management primitive. The system tracks visited states and prunes redundant paths dynamically to optimize resource consumption during deep execution trees.

## Rumours, clearly labelled

It is worth noting unconfirmed claims circulating regarding future model architectures. Specifically, looped transformer designs purportedly form the underlying backbone of unreleased models like **GPT-6 Astra** and Fable 5.2. This claim remains entirely unverified by official sources and should be treated as speculative chatter until official model cards or technical papers are published.

| Item | Status | Basis | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Inkling 2 Mini** | Confirmed | Model card | 26.4B total, 3.4B active parameters |
| **Genie 4 API** | Confirmed | Documentation | Priced at $0.10 per second |
| **GPT-6.2 Astra Defenses** | Confirmed | Security blog | Extraction rate down to 0.2% |
| **Looped GPT-6 / Fable 5.2** | Unconfirmed | Rumour | Speculative architectural overlap |

## Odd finds and small tools

Ecosystem toolchains often house overlooked utilities that streamline daily engineering tasks. The **MiniMind** PyTorch repository stands out as a clean, dependency-light reference implementation for understanding raw tensor manipulations during tokenization and backward passes. Similarly, the **Hallmark** design skill provides an automated guardrail against homogenization in agent-generated frontends, shifting the baseline aesthetic of automated web development.

## What I would try this weekend

I would pull down the **Inkling 2 Mini** weights to benchmark local inference latency on a 32 GB RAM machine, specifically measuring how the triple-pass looped layers affect tokens-per-second compared to standard baseline models of similar active size. Afterward, I would test the **Genie 4** API with a series of architectural blueprint images to see how accurately the physics engine translates static 2D designs into navigable 720p environments.

## Where this leaves us

Architectural experimentation is clearly moving beyond simple parameter stacking toward clever inference-time compute loops and specialized search primitives. While tools like **Inkling 2 Mini** and **Genie 4** offer exciting new capabilities, questions remain regarding their long-term cost scaling and generalization limits in production environments. Developers must weigh these local efficiency gains against the operational complexities of managing new execution topologies.

What custom environment will you test first with the Genie 4 API?

## What actually moved today

The landscape of developer tooling shifted toward tighter local control and autonomous execution loops this week. We are seeing a distinct trend where model weights are kept stable while targeted LoRA adapters and harness updates do the heavy lifting for workflow efficiency. Instead of waiting for massive foundational pre-training runs, the community is rapidly iterating on adapter-based steering and terminal-native UX.

### The shift in developer tooling

Developer workflows are no longer just about generating a snippet of boilerplate or explaining an existing function. Terminal harnesses like **Cline 3.0.75** and **Codex CLI 0.171** are blurring the line between editor extensions and autonomous execution environments. When tools can automatically execute shell commands or manage a TUI workspace sidebar by default, the developer's role shifts from writing code to reviewing execution traces.

### Architectural discipline in agents

At the same time, we are seeing a pushback against chaotic, sprawling agent outputs through structured constraints. The release of the **ub-mode** open-source skill and structured design guides for multi-agent systems using **MCP** proves that software engineering discipline is finding its way back into AI-generated codebases. We are moving past the phase of treating agents as mere text completion oracles and treating them as junior engineers who need guardrails, TDD cycles, and clear architectural patterns.

## The model watch

### Hugging Face Qwen3.8-27B LoRA Adapters

Hugging Face has trained and released specialized LoRA adapters for **Qwen3.8-27B** using reinforcement learning across Pi, OpenCode, and Hermes Agent datasets. These adapters are available under the Apache 2.0 license alongside their GGUF counterparts, making them immediately usable on local hardware setups. The mechanical change here is striking: scores on SWE-bench Pro jumped from 39.2% to 64.7% while the model reduced its tool invocation frequency by 53 to 72 percent. This proves that we can curb unnecessary API calls and looping behaviors through targeted adapter training rather than tweaking system prompts or upgrading to a larger base model. For a developer maintaining a local evaluation harness, re-running your test suites against these new GGUF weights is an easy win to measure real-world reduction in token consumption.

### CLI Harness Updates: Cline, Codex, and Crush

Terminal-based coding interfaces received a flurry of official updates that alter how developers interact with local agents. **Cline CLI 3.0.75** introduced a yolo mode designed to execute terminal commands by default without requiring manual confirmation for every step, speeding up iterative debugging loops significantly. Simultaneously, **Codex CLI 0.171** enabled a TUI workspace sidebar by default with rich file previews and swapped its underlying default model to **GPT-6.2 Sol**, changing the default token generation backend and response pacing. Rounding out the trio, **Crush 0.102** added support for custom system prompt templates, allowing teams to strictly define persona rules for both main agents and nested subagents. These updates demand a re-evaluation of your security boundaries, especially if you experiment with automated execution flags in local development environments.

### Engineering craft and architectural guides

Beyond raw models and CLI flags, workflow discipline saw direct tooling support with the release of the **ub-mode** open-source skill. Designed to enforce Uncle Bob's classic software engineering principles within AI coding loops, it mandates a strict workflow starting with test-driven development, root cause analysis before patching, complexity reduction, and disciplined Git commit formatting. It integrates cleanly with agents like Claude Code and Cursor. Complementing this, Packt Publishing dropped the repository and design guide for *Design Multi-Agent AI Systems Using MCP and A2A*, offering concrete Python-based frameworks for tool use, persistent memory, and multi-agent coordination. Developers looking to build robust agentic pipelines can immediately clone these repositories to adopt standardized MCP communication patterns instead of inventing custom JSON-RPC wrappers from scratch.

## Odd finds and small tools

Amidst the flagship model news and massive harness updates, a few smaller utilities deserve a spotlight for solving niche developer pain points. We spotted a lightweight terminal utility that parses unstructured JSON logs into clean, color-coded tabular output without requiring external Python dependencies. Another small find is a minimalist git-hook generator that automatically strips trailing whitespace and validates conventional commit syntax locally before the pre-push hook even fires. These micro-tools rarely make headlines, but they often save more cumulative developer hours over a sprint than a brand-new reasoning model.

## What I would try this weekend

If you want to poke at these updates without disrupting your main work tree, spin up a local container and pull the **Qwen3.8-27B** GGUF weights alongside the new LoRA adapters. Run a localized evaluation script on a known subset of SWE-bench Pro tasks to verify whether your token usage drops as sharply as the benchmark claims when tool call frequency is reined in. Next, check out the **ub-mode** skill and inject it into your local coding agent configuration. Give it a slightly complex refactoring task where it is forced to write failing tests first, and observe whether it respects the TDD constraint or tries to sneak in a monolithic implementation shortcut. Finally, review your local CLI harness configurations in **Cline** or **Codex** to see if your default permission prompts match your current comfort level with automated terminal execution.

## Where this leaves us

We are landing in a phase of developer tooling where raw model capability is taking a back seat to workflow integration, adapter efficiency, and strict behavioral guardrails. The fact that a LoRA adapter can push **Qwen3.8-27B** past previous baseline ceilings while cutting down tool invocation clutter means we can build faster, cheaper local loops. However, much remains unknown about how these adapters generalize across vastly different proprietary codebases outside of benchmark suites. Autonomous CLI execution modes bring undeniable speed, but they also raise the stakes for local security and accidental state corruption. As we wire up multi-agent systems via **MCP** and enforce strict craftsmanship principles, the real challenge is no longer getting an agent to write code—it is keeping it disciplined enough that you can actually trust the diff.

> **TL;DR** This engineering digest explores Claude helping prove Valiant's conjecture, Baidu's new open weights for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview, and an open-source eBPF shielding tool from OpenAI and Cisco. It also covers Aleph Alpha's latest Mixture of Experts release and recent infrastructure security updates from OpenRouter.

Recent shifts in machine learning engineering are moving past basic chat interfaces and focusing heavily on specialized execution environments, verifiable outputs, and large-scale architectural efficiency. Developers today face a landscape where model weights are larger and more accessible, but runtime security and data retention auditing require much tighter oversight. Understanding these changes means looking closely at how models interact with formal logic, Linux kernels, and distributed inference providers.

## What actually moved today

The boundary between theoretical computer science and practical machine learning shifted noticeably when Anthropic published a major formalization using Claude. At the same time, infrastructure tooling saw significant additions with OpenAI and Cisco releasing Shirudo, an eBPF-based vulnerability mitigation tool. These developments point toward a broader trend where artificial intelligence is increasingly used to reason about and secure low-level system mechanics rather than simply generating natural language prose. Infrastructure stability and verifiable correctness are taking center stage in production environments.

Infrastructure providers are also facing stricter compliance requirements, as evidenced by OpenRouter's recent security audit and subsequent endpoint removals. When inference providers fail to maintain zero data retention guarantees, developers must adapt their data governance strategies immediately. This operational reality demands a rigorous approach to logging, payload inspection, and third-party API dependencies.

## The model watch

### Claude and Valiant's conjecture

Anthropic published a 70-stanza paper paired with a Lean 4 formalization proving Valiant's conjecture regarding VP versus VNP. The core discovery came from an internal research model capable of constructing long-form algebraic proofs. For developers, this demonstrates that current architectures can handle rigorous symbolic logic when paired with automated theorem provers. You might want to re-run your complex logic evals to see how modern models handle multi-step deterministic constraints.

The mechanics of this achievement rely on combining generative inference with strict proof assistants that reject invalid logical leaps. While the paper represents a substantial theoretical milestone, the exact prompt chaining and verification loops used internally remain proprietary. Developers cannot yet replicate this exact automated proving pipeline locally, but the public Lean 4 repository offers valuable insight into how the final proofs were structured and validated.

### ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview and Kolibri 1.1

Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview under the Apache 2.0 license, featuring 280 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window. The model achieves 46.5 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0, making it a compelling option for tasks requiring massive context ingestion. Meanwhile, Aleph Alpha published weights for Kolibri 1.1, a 75 billion parameter Mixture of Experts model optimized specifically for code generation and agentic workflows. Kolibri 1.1 reduces required GPU time by 3.4 times compared to its predecessor while maintaining competitive benchmark metrics.

Both releases give backend engineers new options for local and self-hosted deployments where data privacy is paramount. Evaluating ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview involves provisioning hardware capable of handling high token concurrency, while Kolibri 1.1 offers a more lightweight MoE alternative for routine code synthesis. Developers should benchmark both against their specific domain datasets to determine if the architectural trade-offs align with their latency and throughput requirements.

## Rumours, clearly labelled

Speculation often outpaces official documentation, and several unconfirmed claims are currently circulating across developer communities. These items lack official repository releases, formal paper publications, or verified public endpoints.

| Item | Status | Basis | Verified |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Gemini Carbon availability | Unconfirmed | Google AI Pro plan chatter | No |
| Unreleased frontier models | Unconfirmed | Executive hints and leaks | No |

Treating these claims with caution is essential for maintaining stable system architectures. Relying on unannounced features or unverified endpoints can introduce unexpected breaking changes into production pipelines.

## Odd finds and small tools

Beyond flagship model releases and massive parameter counts, smaller utilities continue to solve highly specific developer pain points. Shirudo, jointly introduced by OpenAI and Cisco, stands out as a practical tool for mitigating vulnerabilities on running Linux servers without requiring system restarts. An integrated AI agent writes a targeted eBPF filter to block active exploit paths while allowing normal application traffic to pass uninterrupted.

This approach bridges the historical gap between vulnerability discovery and emergency patch deployment in production environments. By operating at the kernel level via eBPF, Shirudo minimizes performance overhead while providing immediate runtime protection against zero-day exploits. Developers managing large fleets of Linux instances should review the open-source repository to understand how the generated filters are verified before insertion.

## What I would try this weekend

Testing new open weights is the best way to separate marketing claims from practical utility. I would start by spinning up Aleph Alpha's Kolibri 1.1 to benchmark its code generation speed against existing internal pipelines, measuring both token generation latency and memory overhead. Following that, running a localized evaluation of ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview's million-token context window using a large legacy codebase can reveal how well it handles broad dependency mapping.

For infrastructure security, setting up a staging environment to test eBPF filter generation using the new tooling from OpenAI and Cisco offers a hands-on look at runtime vulnerability mitigation. Observing how the agent constructs filters under simulated attack conditions provides valuable perspective on the current reliability of automated kernel-level defense mechanisms.

## Where this leaves us

We are navigating a phase where model capabilities are expanding into formal verification and kernel-level security, yet fundamental operational risks remain. Data retention incidents on third-party routing platforms remind us that API privacy cannot be taken for granted. While open weights like Kolibri 1.1 and ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview give engineering teams greater control, they also demand deeper local infrastructure expertise.

Many questions remain regarding the long-term reliability of AI-generated security filters and the true cost of hosting massive context windows in production. Balancing innovation with rigorous verification is the only way to build resilient systems moving forward. What specific metric do you prioritize when evaluating a new open-weights model for your team?

## What it is

Mister Download Manager (MDM) is a clean-room, open-source download manager written entirely in Rust. If you have spent years relying on legacy tools like IDM, you know the drill: they are often paid, proprietary, and filled with nag screens. MDM aims to replicate that familiar interface—the toolbar, the categories, the progress windows—but rebuilds it from the ground up using the egui framework for a native, performant experience across Windows, macOS, and Linux.

## Why it matters

Most download managers today are stuck in a cycle of bloatware. They often require licenses, force you into trials, or clutter your system with unnecessary telemetry. MDM shifts the paradigm by offering a lightweight, open-source alternative that doesn't sacrifice speed. Because it is written in Rust, it manages resources efficiently, which is particularly noticeable when handling multiple concurrent downloads or large files. It treats torrents and magnet links as first-class citizens, meaning you don't need a separate client for those tasks.

## Key features

- **Rust-native architecture:** Built for memory safety and high-speed throughput.
- **Universal support:** Handles standard HTTP/HTTPS downloads, magnet links, and .torrent files.
- **Browser integration:** Includes extensions for Firefox, Chrome, Edge, and Brave to intercept downloads automatically.
- **Cross-platform:** Works natively on Windows, macOS, and Linux (including support for X11 and Wayland sessions).
- **No-bloat design:** No ads, no trials, and no sign-up requirements.

## Quick start

If you are on Windows, you can install it using the Windows Package Manager (winget). Open your terminal and run:

```bash
winget install AhmedNefzaoui.MisterDownloadManager
```

For other platforms, you can download the latest binaries directly from the GitHub releases page. Linux users can choose between .deb, .rpm, or AppImage formats depending on their distribution.

## Who should try it

This tool is for anyone who frequently manages large downloads and is tired of the 'nagware' model of traditional download managers. If you are a developer who appreciates open-source software and wants a tool that respects your system resources, MDM is a great fit. It is also ideal for users who want to consolidate their HTTP and torrent downloading into a single, unified interface.

## Verdict

MDM is a refreshing take on a utility category that has been stagnant for years. It doesn't try to reinvent the wheel; it simply makes the wheel faster, free, and open-source. While it is still a relatively young project, it is stable enough for daily use and provides a clean, performant experience that makes proprietary alternatives feel obsolete. If you are looking for a reliable, no-nonsense downloader, this is the one to grab.

## What it is

Spaceship IDE is an experimental interface designed to challenge the standard chat-box paradigm of LLM interaction. Instead of sending a prompt and waiting for a static response, the project treats the model's output as a continuous stream that you can manipulate on the fly. It utilizes techniques like speculative generation to keep the UI responsive, allowing you to adjust the model's trajectory while it is still generating text.

## Why it matters

Most current developer tools for LLMs are built around the request-response cycle. You send a prompt, you wait, you get a result, and if it is wrong, you start over. As inference speeds increase, this cycle becomes a bottleneck. Spaceship IDE explores what happens when we treat LLM generation as a live, steerable stream. By decomposing tasks into eigenvectors and using attention locks, it moves the user from a passive observer to an active pilot.

## Key features

* **Real-time vector steering:** Decompose tasks into independent components and tune them individually to influence the incoming text.
* **Attention lock:** Force the LLM to prioritize specific phrases, biasing its future behavior mid-generation.
* **Speculative generation:** The engine manages aggressive caching and invalidation to maintain a responsive, 60 FPS-style interaction feel.
* **Visual focus monitor:** A UI element that visualizes what the LLM is paying attention to, helping you guide the model toward relevant information.
* **Local-first keys:** API keys for providers like Cerebras and Gemini are stored in your browser's local storage, keeping them out of the server-side logs.

## Quick start

To explore the interface, clone the repository and run it locally:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/chuanqisun/spaceship
```

You can also try the live simulator directly in your browser at the project's homepage.

## Who should try it

This project is for developers, UI/UX researchers, and AI enthusiasts who are interested in the future of human-computer interaction. If you are building tools that require fine-grained control over LLM output, or if you are simply tired of the standard chat interface, this provides a compelling look at alternative interaction models.

## Verdict

Spaceship IDE is a fascinating experiment that successfully demonstrates how we might interact with AI when latency is no longer the primary constraint. It is not a production-ready tool for your daily coding tasks, but it is a vital conceptual launchpad for anyone thinking about how to build better, more intuitive AI interfaces. If you want to see what the next generation of LLM tooling might look like, it is worth a look.

generated.article_markdown:
## What it is

Edge0 is an inference framework designed to solve the memory wall for local LLMs. Instead of trying to cram an entire model into VRAM—which is usually impossible for anything over 70B parameters on consumer hardware—Edge0 uses a latent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. It streams weights from your SSD on demand, using a router that predicts which experts are needed for the next step of inference. This allows you to run massive models, like the 145B parameter variants, on a single NVIDIA GPU.

## Why it matters

For a long time, local inference was a trade-off between parameter count and hardware cost. If you wanted the reasoning capabilities of a 100B+ model, you were effectively forced to the cloud. Edge0 changes the math by treating your storage as an extension of your memory. By predicting the computational load ahead of time, the framework keeps the GPU busy with only the necessary experts, effectively decoupling the model size from your physical VRAM capacity.

## Key features

- **Massive Scale:** Runs 145B parameter models on a single 24GB NVIDIA GPU using latent MoE.
- **Weight Streaming:** Streams model weights from SSD to bypass VRAM limitations during inference.
- **Predictive Routing:** Predicts computational load steps ahead to optimize sparse expert activation.
- **Unified Interface:** Provides a unified C++ API and CLI for serving and chat applications.
- **Optimized Formats:** Supports Q3_K and NVFP4 quantization formats for optimized local performance.

## Quick start

To start a local server for your model, use the `edge0-infer` CLI:

```bash
edge0-infer serve --model path/to/model
```

## Who should try it

This is for developers who are building local agent workloads and are hitting the ceiling of what their hardware can handle. If you have an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 13) on Linux or Windows and need the reasoning power of a 145B model without the latency of an API call, this is the tool to use. If you are working on Apple Silicon or mobile, note that these platforms currently rely on the legacy engine, so you won't get the same performance benefits as the 145B/120B series.

## Verdict

Edge0 is a pragmatic solution to the VRAM bottleneck. It is a solid choice if you have an NVIDIA GPU and need massive model reasoning locally. However, skip it if you are strictly on Apple Silicon or mobile, as those platforms rely on the older, less feature-rich engine.

## What it is

rust-anything is a command-line tool and agent-assisted workflow designed to help developers rewrite applications in Rust piece by piece. Instead of risking a hazardous big-bang rewrite of a Node.js, Python, Go, C, Ruby, or Java codebase, it captures the actual inputs, outputs, and edge-case behavior of your current implementation. You or your AI coding agent write the Rust port, and the framework replays the recorded execution traces to ensure the new code behaves identically.

## Why it matters

Rewriting production software usually forces an impossible choice: maintain an unmaintainable legacy codebase or bet the business on a risky rewrite that introduces silent regressions. This project sidesteps that trap by treating the original implementation as an oracle. Because every single run is recorded and checked against the Rust rewrite, you can replace hot paths or entire servers with high confidence.

## Key features

- Record original application behavior on edge cases and semantic traps to establish a baseline.
- Bridge generated Rust crates with wrappers so callers retain the original API structure.
- Replay thousands of recorded test cases against the Rust port to verify identical outputs.
- Profile codebases to identify hot paths and loops worth moving out of interpreted runtimes.
- Lift fully verified components and dependencies into a standalone pure Rust application.

## Quick start

```sh
cargo install rust-anything
rust-anything setup
```

## Who should try it

This tool fits teams maintaining performance-sensitive services or libraries in higher-level languages who want the memory safety and speed of Rust without risking a full rewrite.

## Verdict

It provides a remarkably disciplined path to modernizing legacy codebases, though its success ultimately depends on the quality of your recordings and the Rust code you write.

## What it is

Exact is a cross-platform application runtime that separates your interface definition from your data logic. Instead of building a webview-based app or managing separate native codebases, you describe your UI in a declarative language called Contract. This contract is compiled into a plan that executes on a lightweight runtime. On the web, this is a 20 KB module that drives the DOM; on macOS, iOS, and Linux, it is a Rust-based runner that uses native controls or a GPU painter to render your app.

## Why it matters

Most cross-platform tools rely on JavaScript bridges or heavy webviews, which often lead to performance bottlenecks and inconsistent behavior across platforms. Exact bypasses these by using a Rust-based layout kernel that computes UI boxes using CSS rules. Because the runtime is designed to be driven by AI agents, you can write tests that run identically on the web, macOS, and iOS without needing to manage separate test evaluators or handle flaky timing issues.

## Key features

- **Native Rendering:** Uses AppKit, UIKit, or a GPU painter instead of webviews.
- **Agent-First API:** Includes ten standardized operations (like `tap`, `type`, and `screenshot`) to drive testing across all hosts.
- **Performance:** Designed for sub-100ms cold starts by avoiding heavy JavaScript execution before the first pixel.
- **Declarative UI:** Uses a small, typed language that fits within an AI context window, making it easier for agents to generate and maintain code.

## Quick start

To get started, ensure you have Rust, Bun, and Xcode installed, then run the following commands:

```sh
bun scripts/exact.mjs setup
bun scripts/exact.mjs new my-app
```

## Who should try it

Exact is for developers who are comfortable with early-stage, pre-1.0 tooling and want to avoid the overhead of traditional cross-platform frameworks. ## Verdict

Exact is an ambitious project that trades the flexibility of standard webviews for strict, native-first performance. It is not for those who need API stability or a mature ecosystem today, but it offers a compelling vision for how we might build and test apps in an AI-assisted future.

## What it is

Moli is a production-ready headless browser written in Rust designed specifically for AI agents, web crawling, and automated testing workloads. Rather than forcing continuous visual rendering, it treats the native DOM and style state as the primary source of truth, performing layout and software paint operations strictly on demand.

## Why it matters

Most browser automation tasks require page structure rather than a rendered visual viewport. Traditional tools continuously maintain a visual state that wastes CPU cycles and memory. Moli optimizes this cost model by reading runtime state directly for text extraction, DOM queries, and JavaScript execution, only triggering box construction and Taffy layout when visual outputs like screenshots or coordinate inputs are explicitly requested.

## Key features

- Execute CDP, WebDriver Classic, and WebDriver BiDi through a single unified automation binary.
- Dump pages directly to HTML, Markdown, JSON, or compact semantic text trees via CLI.
- Run full V8 JavaScript, CSS cascade, Fetch/XHR/WebSocket, and profile-scoped storage.
- Enable full box construction and Taffy layout on demand by passing the --layout flag.
- Connect Playwright directly over Chrome DevTools Protocol without extra drivers.

## Quick start

On Linux or macOS:

```sh
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL \
  https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.sh | sh
```

On Windows, run in PowerShell:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.ps1 | iex"
```

## Who should try it

Developers building autonomous web agents, heavy scraping pipelines, or automated test suites who want to reduce the resource overhead associated with running traditional browser binaries.

## Verdict

Moli offers a pragmatic architecture for text-heavy agent workflows and scraping pipelines, though teams requiring complex browser extensions should test thoroughly before migrating.

## What it is

Kiri is a container runtime written in Rust designed to be a drop-in replacement for Docker Desktop. It implements the Docker Engine API, meaning your existing `docker` CLI, Compose files, and build scripts continue to work without modification. Instead of running a heavy, persistent VM in the background, Kiri uses a lightweight architecture that keeps the daemon footprint around 15MB and puts the VM to sleep after 60 seconds of inactivity.

## Why it matters

For many developers, Docker Desktop has become a resource hog. It consumes significant memory even when idle and often suffers from slow startup times. Kiri addresses this by prioritizing efficiency. By waking up in about 0.15 seconds and keeping the daemon small, it removes the friction of waiting for your container environment to be ready. It also adds quality-of-life features like automatic local domains with HTTPS and built-in Kubernetes support, making it a practical tool for local development.

## Key features

* **Fast Startup:** Containers start in approximately 2.5ms via the Docker API.
* **Resource Efficient:** The daemon stays at ~15MB and sleeps when idle to save battery.
* **Local Domains:** Automatically generates `http://<name>.kiri.local` for containers and Compose services, complete with HTTPS.
* **Kubernetes Ready:** Includes a single-node k3s cluster accessible via `kiri k8s`.
* **Easy Migration:** Use `kiri import` to bring your existing images, volumes, and containers over from Docker Desktop or OrbStack.

## Quick start

First, install Kiri via your package manager or the website. Once installed, you can immediately start using it with your existing Docker commands:

```bash
docker --context kiri run --rm alpine echo hello
```

You can also use the `kiri` CLI directly for advanced features:

```bash
kiri compose up -d
kiri k8s start
```

## Who should try it

Kiri is ideal for developers who are frustrated by the resource usage of Docker Desktop but rely on the Docker ecosystem. If you are working on a laptop where battery life and memory are at a premium, or if you simply want a faster feedback loop when spinning up containers, this is a strong candidate.

## Verdict

Kiri is a mature, performant alternative to the standard Docker Desktop experience. It is well-suited for daily development tasks and offers a noticeable improvement in startup speed and resource management. While it handles most standard use cases, as with any container runtime switch, you should verify that your specific volume mount configurations and networking setups are supported before making it your primary environment.

## What it is

SoduWork is a self-hosted engine designed to move AI agent interactions beyond simple chat threads. Instead of treating AI as a conversational partner, it treats AI as an execution engine. It forces a structured workflow: you submit a request with specific acceptance criteria, an agent executes the work, a second agent reviews the result, and a human must sign off before the task is considered complete.

## Why it matters

Most developer AI tooling today is built around the chat interface. While great for brainstorming, this model fails when you need reliable, repeatable output. You end up with 'prompt drift,' where the AI forgets constraints, or 'knowledge loss,' where a perfect prompt chain is buried in a chat history you can't easily reference later. SoduWork addresses this by turning successful agent interactions into versioned, reusable plugins that your entire team can access.

## Key features

- **Dual-agent verification:** The system uses one agent to execute tasks and another to review the output against your acceptance criteria.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** Tasks remain open until a human explicitly signs off, ensuring the AI doesn't just 'hallucinate' that it finished the job.
- **Plugin system:** Capture successful AI interactions as reusable, versioned plugins for team-wide use.
- **Model-agnostic:** Supports switching between different model harnesses (e.g., DeepSeek, Qwen, Codex) mid-conversation.
- **Self-hosted deployment:** Runs via Docker, keeping data and governance within your own infrastructure.

## Quick start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/mdiri-ai/SoduWork
cd SoduWork
```

## Who should try it

## Verdict

SoduWork is a practical step toward agentic maturity. It is honest about the fact that AI needs oversight, not just more prompts. The app relies on the File System Access API to rewrite itself when saved. Clone the repository from GitHub and open the main HTML file in any modern browser to start building local-first presentations.

## When not to use it

Avoid this tool if you need heavy mobile editing capabilities, as touch-based slide manipulation remains awkward.

generated.article_markdown:
## What it is

OpenFilm is a framework that turns standard coding agents into video editors. Instead of treating video as a black-box binary file, it treats a project as a folder containing a film.html file. This file uses web technologies—CSS, JS, and HTML—to define tracks, clips, and timing. Because the project is essentially a web page, you can inspect and modify it using standard developer tools.

## Why it matters

Most AI video tools are opaque; you prompt them, they render a file, and if you want a change, you have to re-prompt and hope for the best. OpenFilm changes this dynamic by introducing an overrides system. When an agent generates a scene, your manual edits (like moving a text element or changing a color) are stored as overrides. This means the agent can continue to build on the project without wiping out your specific tweaks.

## Key features

- Treats video projects as web pages using film.html for layout and timing.
- Supports manual overrides for text, color, and position that persist through AI regeneration.
- Integrates with existing coding agents like Claude Code or Codex for automated asset assembly.
- Provides four distinct editors: Screening, Edit, Canvas, and Color.
- Exports timelines compatible with professional tools like DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro.

## Quick start

To add the OpenFilm skill to your existing coding agent (requires Node 22.2+ and ffmpeg), run the following command:

```bash
npx skills add openfilm/openfilm
```

## Who should try it

This is for developers who are already comfortable with coding agents and want to bring that same workflow to video production. If you are tired of fighting AI generators that don't allow for precise, granular control, this provides a way to maintain that control without sacrificing the speed of AI generation.

## Verdict

A solid choice for devs who want to treat video like code. It is highly effective if you are comfortable working with web-based project structures. If you prefer traditional non-linear editors (NLEs) and want to avoid the overhead of managing code-based projects, you might find this approach adds unnecessary complexity.

## What it is

Pixelfx is a library of 244 pixel art effects—fire, melee, weather, UI, and more—where every effect is defined as a small piece of JavaScript code. Instead of managing hundreds of static sprite sheets, you treat your VFX as data. You can run them directly in a browser canvas, or use the included CLI tools to render them into transparent PNG sprite sheets with Aseprite-compatible JSON metadata for use in engines like Godot, Unity, or Phaser.

Beyond just the visuals, the project includes an "acting" system. It understands that a good hit effect isn't just the explosion—it's the wind-up, the freeze on contact, and the recovery. You can chain these moves together to create combat sequences that feel responsive rather than floaty.

## Why it matters

If you have ever spent an entire weekend redrawing a sword slash because the timing felt slightly off, you know the pain of static pixel art assets. Pixelfx changes the medium. Because the effects are code, you can change the palette, the timing, or the scale without ever opening an image editor. 

This is particularly useful when combined with the included Claude Code skill. You can ask an agent to "make this hit effect punchier" or "add a wind-up to this spell," and it iterates on the code rather than trying to manipulate pixels directly. It turns the VFX pipeline into a feedback loop of code, render, and refine.

## Key features

*   **Extensive Library:** 244 effects covering categories like arcane, sci-fi, nature, and UI.
*   **Engine Agnostic:** While it runs natively in JS, the CLI tools allow you to export sprite sheets for any engine that supports Aseprite-style JSON.
*   **Palette Control:** Every effect accepts a palette array, allowing you to recolor fire or magic effects programmatically without touching the source code.
*   **Acting System:** Built-in support for character poses, wind-ups, and hit-stops, making it easier to sync VFX with combat logic.
*   **AI Integration:** A dedicated Claude Code plugin allows for iterative generation and refinement of new effects.

## Quick start

To get started, install the package directly from GitHub:

```bash
npm i github:patch-gg/pixelfx
```

Once installed, you can import effects directly into your project or use the CLI tools to export assets for other engines.

## Who should try it

This is a great fit for solo indie developers or small teams working on browser-based games who want to move fast. If you are already comfortable with JavaScript and want to automate the tedious parts of VFX creation, this will save you a significant amount of time. If you are strictly a non-coder artist, the learning curve for the JS-based authoring might be steeper than traditional tools.

## Verdict

Pixelfx is a smart, pragmatic approach to a common game dev bottleneck. It won't replace a dedicated animator for complex character work, but for the hundreds of small effects that clutter a game, it is an efficient, highly customizable solution.

## What it is

Peach is a local-first media management platform designed to solve the fragmentation problem of modern video collections. Instead of forcing you to upload your data to a proprietary cloud service or rely on a rigid, black-box media server, Peach acts as an indexing layer that sits directly on top of your existing file storage. It supports a wide range of backends, including local drives, SMB shares, and cloud storage mounts, allowing you to treat disparate sources as a single, cohesive library.

At its core, the tool is a metadata scraper. It scans your media directories, identifies video codes, and automatically fetches relevant information—titles, performers, studios, and cover art—from external sources. Crucially, it respects your local edits, ensuring that your manual adjustments to metadata are preserved even when the scraper updates its own records.

## Why it matters

For developers and power users, the status quo of media management is often frustrating. You either deal with manual file renaming and spreadsheet tracking, or you surrender your data to a commercial service that might disappear or change its terms tomorrow. Peach addresses this by prioritizing local-first architecture. Your watch history, tags, and library configuration remain on your machine. This approach provides a level of durability and privacy that is increasingly rare in the current ecosystem of 'smart' media tools.

## Key features

*   **Unified Library Management**: Mounts local, SMB, and cloud storage into one interface, eliminating the need to switch between different file explorers.
*   **Metadata Persistence**: Scrapes titles, performers, and studios while allowing you to override and keep your own edits.
*   **Performer Tracking**: Tracks creator updates and manages want lists, helping you discover new content without relying on algorithmic feeds.
*   **Resource Monitoring**: Includes a dedicated task center that lets you pause, resume, and monitor background tasks, including CPU and GPU usage.
*   **Extensible Playback**: Supports external players, subtitle management, and timeline previews, giving you control over the viewing experience.

## Quick start

To get started with the source code, ensure you have Git, uv, and Python 3.14+ installed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/peach-mitao/peach && cd peach
# Follow docs/OPERATIONS.md for dependency installation and setup
```

Alternatively, pre-built installers for Windows and macOS are available in the project's releases section.

## Who should try it

Peach is ideal for users who have outgrown simple file folders and want a structured, searchable library without the overhead of enterprise-grade media servers. If you are comfortable configuring your own storage mounts and value data sovereignty over convenience-first cloud services, this is a strong candidate for your stack.

## Verdict

Peach is a highly effective tool for those who prioritize local control and organization. It does not try to be a 'set it and forget it' solution; it requires some initial setup, but the payoff is a clean, unified library that you actually own. Skip it if you are looking for a zero-configuration, cloud-native experience.

## What it is

Xbox2Windows is a research project focused on static recompilation, moving software designed for the Xbox Series X/S (Scarlett) architecture to x64 Windows. Rather than emulating the hardware at runtime, it attempts to translate the binary's x64 machine code into C++ and convert the console-specific gfx1013 shaders into desktop-compatible DXIL. It uses a shim-based approach to redirect D3D12 calls and memory allocations, allowing the recompiled code to interact with the Windows environment.

## Why it matters

Bridging the gap between console-specific binaries and desktop execution is a significant challenge in reverse engineering and systems research. This project provides a transparent look at how one might map console-specific graphics pipelines and memory management to standard PC APIs. By providing tools to compare native, mapped, and recompiled builds, it allows developers to verify if the translation layer is producing identical results at the pixel and byte level.

## Key features

*   **Machine Code Translation:** Converts x64 machine code into C++ for native compilation.
*   **Shader Mapping:** Translates gfx1013 shaders into standard desktop DXIL.
*   **Verification Suite:** Includes tests that validate output against native Windows, mapped PE, and AOT builds to ensure pixel-perfect parity.
*   **D3D12 Compatibility:** Implements shims for D3D12 root signatures, heap allocation, and software rendering.
*   **Offline Inspection:** Provides tools to inspect PE package imports and export closures without needing to execute the binary.

## Quick start

Ensure you have Python 3.11+ and the Visual Studio Desktop development with C++ workload installed. Then run:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/R0Y00/Xbox2Windows.git
cd Xbox2Windows
.\tools\dev.ps1
cmake --preset dev
cmake --build --preset dev
```

## Who should try it

This project is for developers and researchers who want to study binary translation and shader architecture. If you are interested in how console-specific graphics calls can be shimmed to run on Windows, this provides a concrete, documented codebase to explore. It is not intended for end-users looking to run retail games, as full game startup and menu navigation are not yet supported.

## Verdict

Xbox2Windows is a highly technical research sandbox. It is excellent for those who want to understand the mechanics of static recompilation and binary mapping. However, if you are looking for a functional emulator to play games, you should skip this project, as it is currently focused on low-level diagnostic and architectural research.

## Why it matters

When working with local AI models, the gap between 'reported usage' and 'actual allocation' is often massive. * **LLM Insight:** Specifically designed to surface model weights and KV-cache usage, making it easier to see how much memory your current prompt context is consuming.
* **Container Awareness:** Automatically pairs containerized GPU processes with host-level metrics, solving the common issue where Docker hides process-specific GPU activity.
* **Zero-Config Setup:** Can be installed via `uv` or `pipx`, or run as a portable binary on Windows and Linux without requiring complex driver toolkits.
* **Scriptable Output:** Includes a `--json` flag, enabling you to pipe GPU metrics into other monitoring or logging systems.

The easiest way to get started is using `uv` to install the package directly into an isolated environment:

```powershell
uv tool install gputaskman
gputaskman
```

If you prefer not to install Python, you can download the portable Windows or Linux binaries directly from the project's GitHub releases page.

gputaskman is a highly practical utility that solves a very specific pain point in the local AI development stack. It is transparent about its experimental nature and limitations, but the visibility it provides is unmatched by generic system monitors. It is a must-have for your local dev toolkit.

It operates by hooking into the existing Android TV or Tizen/webOS input management, effectively acting as a lightweight shell that runs at a consistent 60 fps. ## What it is

CADCraft is a 2D and 3D computer-aided design application built entirely in Rust. Unlike many modern CAD tools that rely on Electron or heavy web-view wrappers, CADCraft is a native binary that prioritizes performance and a classic, command-line-driven drafting experience. It handles standard drafting operations—lines, polylines, circles, arcs, and complex modifications like trim and extend—using the keyboard-centric workflow that many professionals have used for decades.

## Why it matters

For developers and engineers, the biggest hurdle with traditional CAD software is the lack of true programmability. Most legacy tools are built as GUI-first silos where automation is an afterthought or locked behind expensive enterprise tiers. CADCraft changes this by treating the command line as the primary interface. Because every action is a command, the software is inherently scriptable. By integrating the Model Context Protocol (MCP), it allows AI agents to inspect, modify, and generate drawings programmatically, bridging the gap between design and code.

## Key features

- Native performance: Built in Rust with egui, it runs natively on macOS, Windows, Linux, and FreeBSD without the resource usage of Electron.
- File compatibility: Native DXF read/write (R12–2018) and DWG support via the acadrust library.
- Agent-ready: Built from the ground up for automation, allowing agents to drive the software via MCP or a JSON control channel.
- Familiar workflow: Supports standard drafting habits like object snaps, polar tracking, ortho, and direct distance entry.
- Web-capable: Includes a WebAssembly build for running directly in the browser.

## Quick start

To get started with the local build, ensure you have Rust 1.95 or later installed:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/storytold/cadcraft
cd cadcraft
cargo run --release -p cadcraft -- --sample
```

Once open, you can interact with the command line by typing commands like `line`, `circle`, or `offset` directly.

## Who should try it

This is for anyone tired of bloated, proprietary CAD suites who wants a lightweight, scriptable alternative. If you are a developer looking to integrate CAD generation into a pipeline, or an engineer who prefers a keyboard-driven workflow, this is a strong candidate. However, if your daily work depends on specialized, third-party plugins from legacy CAD vendors, you will likely find those missing here.

## Verdict

CADCraft is a refreshing, performance-oriented take on CAD. It is currently in early development, so expect some rough edges, but its commitment to open standards and agent-driven automation makes it a project worth watching for anyone who wants to treat their drafting process as code.

## What it is

## How it works
NOIR utilizes the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to interface with the device. Instead of downloading and decompiling full APK binaries—which is resource-intensive—it parses installed package manifests and DEX headers directly. It performs lightweight string analysis to identify network URLs and cross-references them against known SDK telemetry signatures to generate risk assessments.

- **Permission Mapping:** Connects app permissions to specific data types like location, contacts, and storage.
- **Endpoint Extraction:** Identifies network URLs embedded within the app structure.
- **Manifest Analysis:** Parses binary AndroidManifest.xml files to find unprotected exported components.
- **Deep Inspection:** Supports optional integration with jadx for targeted decompilation when deeper runtime analysis is required.

## Getting started
Ensure you have ADB installed and your device connected with USB debugging enabled. Clone the repository and build the project using Gradle:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Verlintas/NOIR
cd NOIR
./gradlew build
```

Run the tool to begin scanning your device's installed packages.

## When not to use it
NOIR is a diagnostic tool for security professionals and developers. It is not designed for casual users looking for a one-click privacy "fix" or a firewall solution. It provides data for analysis, not automated blocking or remediation.

OhMyGame is an open-source, Electron-based studio designed to consolidate the fragmented game development workflow. Instead of jumping between an IDE, a 3D modeler, a sound editor, and a browser, you use this single application as a canvas. You connect your own LLM provider via API keys, and the agent takes over the heavy lifting: it drafts design documents, writes the code, generates assets, and even runs the game to test for bugs.

## Why it matters

Game development is notoriously context-heavy. A simple prototype often requires you to maintain a complex pipeline of assets and code across multiple specialized applications. OhMyGame attempts to solve this by creating a unified environment where the AI agent understands the entire project state. By bringing the agent into the studio, it can handle the repetitive tasks of asset generation and integration, allowing you to focus on the game design itself.

## Key features

* **Automated dev loop:** The agent handles design, coding, playtesting, and debugging in a continuous cycle.
* **Unified asset canvas:** Generate 3D models, audio, and images directly on the canvas, keeping everything organized.

* **Plugin ecosystem:** Extends functionality to existing engines like Godot, Unity, Unreal, and Blender.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/WhiteTowerAI/ohmygame.git
```

This tool is ideal for solo developers and prototypers who want to build web-based games quickly. If you are tired of the friction caused by switching between five different creative tools just to iterate on a single mechanic, this provides a much-needed consolidation. However, if you are deeply entrenched in a specific engine like Unity or Unreal, you might find this more useful as a companion tool for prototyping rather than a full replacement for your existing production environment.

## Verdict

OhMyGame is a promising step toward making game development more accessible and less fragmented. It is not a magic bullet—you still need to manage your own API keys and model providers—but it successfully removes the operational overhead that often kills a project before it gets off the ground. generated.article_markdown:
## What it is
HatchZip is an archive extractor designed for a specific, annoying problem: running out of disk space while trying to unpack a file that is almost as large as your remaining free space. Traditional extractors like `unzip` or 7-Zip require enough space to hold both the source archive and the uncompressed output simultaneously. HatchZip flips this by processing the archive from the end and truncating the source file as it goes, effectively reusing the space the archive occupied for the files being extracted.

## Why it matters
If you work with large datasets, game assets, or virtual machine images, you have likely hit the "disk full" error mid-extraction. Usually, this forces you to clear space, move files to external drives, or delete other projects. HatchZip solves this by managing the disk footprint dynamically. It checks if the extraction will fit before starting and maintains a safety margin, ensuring you don't end up with a corrupted, half-extracted mess if you run out of space.

## Key features
- **In-place extraction:** Supports ZIP, 7z, RAR, and tar, shrinking the source archive as files are extracted.
- **Crash-safe:** If the process is interrupted, it can resume where it left off without data loss.
- **Pre-flight checks:** Calculates whether the extraction will fit before modifying any files.
- **Filesystem optimization:** Leverages hole punching on supported filesystems (ext4, XFS, btrfs) to reclaim space more efficiently.
- **Dual interface:** Provides both a GUI with OS context menu integration and a command-line interface for automation.

## Quick start
For Linux and macOS, you can install the CLI tool directly:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xevrion/hatchzip/main/install.sh | sh
```

For Windows, you can download the installer or portable executable from the project's release page. Once installed, it integrates into your file explorer context menu for right-click extractions.

## Who should try it
This tool is for anyone who frequently deals with large archives on constrained storage. If you are a developer managing large datasets or a gamer dealing with massive compressed assets, this will save you from constant disk management headaches. If you have massive amounts of free storage and rarely deal with archives near your disk capacity, the standard tools you already have are likely sufficient.

## Verdict
HatchZip is a specialized tool that does one thing very well. It is not trying to replace your entire archive management suite, but it is the right choice when you are up against your disk's limits. It is reliable, safe, and solves a genuine pain point in daily development workflows.

## What it is

HatchZip is a free, open-source archive extractor written in Rust that unpacks compressed files in-place. By processing archives from the end and truncating the source file as data is successfully written, it eliminates the traditional double-space requirement for extraction.

## How it works

Standard extractors read a compressed file and write a brand-new uncompressed copy, requiring free space equal to the archive plus the extracted contents. HatchZip manages this differently by reading and writing chunks while shrinking the source file simultaneously. It also supports filesystem hole punching on ext4, XFS, and btrfs for extra efficiency, and includes a crash-safe design that permits resuming interrupted operations.

## Key features

- In-place extraction for ZIP, 7z, RAR, and tar archives
- Crash-safe design with resume capability
- Pre-extraction space checks
- Filesystem hole punching on Linux filesystems
- Desktop GUI with context menu integration and CLI tool

## Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub and build it using Cargo:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip
cd hatchzip
cargo build --release
```

## When not to use it

Skip this utility if your machine has abundant storage space and you never encounter disk capacity warnings during file extraction.

# XCL – Xbox Series X|S → Windows compatibility layer

[![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-join%20the%20server-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/xcl)
**Discord: <https://discord.gg/xcl>**

XCL is a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X|S (GDK) games you own on a Windows PC - in the spirit of Wine/Proton. There is no CPU emulation: the game's x64 code runs natively, and XCL provides its own, independently written implementations of the console system libraries the PC does not have (`kernelx.dll`, XGameRuntime, `d3d12_xs.dll`, …). The console's GPU code (RDNA2 machine code) is recompiled into PC shaders (HLSL → DXIL).

XCL works only on unpacked game files you already own. It does not download, decrypt or unpack game packages (XVC / MSIXVC) and contains nothing for circumventing DRM. The repository holds no code, headers or binaries from the console SDK, no keys and no game data; the Windows components XCL relies on (XGameRuntime, XAudio2, D3D12, DXC) come from your own system or the public Windows SDK and are not distributed with XCL.

queue.description: Progress notes for running Xbox Series X|S builds on PC (TomBox + rage9)
queue.name: xbox-emulator
queue.readme_excerpt:
# Xbox Emulator

**Running the Xbox Series X|S library on PC. A continuation of [drycheetah84/TomBox](https://github.com/drycheetah84/TomBox).**

The runtime reimplements the console's platform layer (Xbox-flavoured Direct3D 12, precompiled RDNA2 shaders, unified-memory textures, system libraries) so dumped, already-decrypted Xbox Series X|S builds run as normal Windows processes. It is not tied to any single title. This repo tracks our continuation — new titles brought up, platform calls extended, shader stages unlocked.

Uses legally obtained, already-decrypted dumps. The runtime does no key extraction or package decryption.

**Source code:** the emulator's Rust workspace is in this repo: [`crates/`](crates/), [`tools/`](tools/) and `Cargo.toml`. It contains no game files, binaries or build output.

**Contributing:** pull requests are welcome, especially console library functions still marked missing in the [library map](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md). See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Licensed GPL-3.0-or-later (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). Releases before this change remain available under MIT OR Apache-2.0.
